title: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
summary: How Coconut lets an LLM reason by feeding its last hidden state back as input: the mechanism, the iCoT-style curriculum, latent breadth-first search on ProsQA, and pause tokens vs recurrent depth.
outcomes: Explain why sampling a token at every reasoning step loses information and forces early commitment
Trace how Coconut builds input sequences in latent mode and count the forward passes it needs
Construct the training sequence and loss mask for any curriculum stage given c and the step count
Explain how one continuous thought can hold several frontier nodes and why delaying commitment helps planning
Compare Coconut with pause tokens, filler tokens, iCoT and recurrent depth on cost, depth and auditability

lessons.title: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck

blocks.md: Recall from how LLMs are trained: a decoder-only model reads a sequence of token embeddings, runs it through its layers, and predicts the next token. **Chain-of-thought (CoT)** means the model writes intermediate reasoning steps as ordinary tokens before the answer. Wei et al. (2022) showed that prompting a 540B-parameter model with just eight worked examples of such steps reached state-of-the-art accuracy on GSM8K, a set of grade-school math word problems.

Why does writing help at all? A transformer has a fixed number of layers, so one forward pass can do only a bounded amount of sequential computation. When an output token is fed back as the next input, the next pass can build on it. Theory papers cited by Coconut (Feng et al. 2023) describe this as CoT raising the **effective depth** of the model. The written tokens are the model's scratch memory.

Hao et al. (FAIR at Meta), the authors of **Coconut** (Chain of Continuous Thought), argue that words are a poor medium for that scratch memory. Most tokens in a reasoning chain exist for fluency, a few critical tokens need real planning, yet every token gets about the same compute. Watch where the information goes in one step of decoding.

blocks.title: The decode loop and Coconut's shortcut

scenes.caption: Ordinary chain-of-thought decoding. One forward pass turns the input vector into a hidden state, the LM head turns it into a distribution, one token is sampled, and its embedding becomes the next input.
The bottleneck. Everything the pass computed must squeeze through one discrete choice. A GPT-2 token identifies one of 50,257 entries, at most about 15.6 bits, and sampling commits to it.
Coconut in latent mode: skip the LM head, the sampling and the lookup. The last hidden state itself is placed in the next input slot. Nothing is discretized, so the whole chain stays differentiable.
After the <eot> marker the model returns to language mode and the normal loop resumes to write the answer. The latent steps leave no tokens in the output.

blocks.caption: A sampled GPT-2 token names one vocabulary entry. The hidden state it was sampled from is a 768-dimensional real vector. This compares raw capacity only, not how much useful information the model actually stores.

blocks.md: The loop also forces a **commitment**. If the model is unsure whether step 2 should go left or right in a search problem, it must still emit one token, and every later step is conditioned on that choice. The hidden state just before sampling could have kept both options alive.

Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you take a model trained only with ordinary next-token prediction and, at inference, simply feed its last hidden state back as the next input. What do you expect?
blocks.reveal: Expect it to fail. The input layer was trained only on vectors from the embedding table, and a last hidden state (taken after the final normalization layer) is a kind of input the model never saw in training. Nothing taught it what a useful thought looks like. Coconut therefore needs a **training procedure**, the subject of lesson 3.

blocks.md: Coconut's one change: in latent mode, the next input embedding is the previous position's last hidden state instead of the embedding of a sampled token.

blocks.question: In one step of ordinary CoT decoding, which operation discards the most information about the model's internal state?
options: The attention layers, because they average over earlier positions
Sampling a single token from softmax(W h), since only its identity is passed on
The final layer normalization before the LM head
The positional encoding added to the next input
blocks.explain: The next pass sees only e(x) for the one sampled token, a vector chosen from a fixed table of 50,257 rows. Everything else in the 768-dimensional h(t), including how probable the alternatives were, is dropped. Attention and normalization transform information but pass a full vector on.

blocks.question: Why does writing reasoning tokens let a fixed-depth transformer solve problems it cannot solve in one pass?
options: Generated tokens are fed back as inputs, so later passes can build on earlier results, increasing effective serial depth
Longer outputs give the attention softmax a sharper distribution
Each written token adds new trainable parameters at inference
The KV cache stores the answer before it is written
blocks.explain: Each pass has bounded depth L. Feeding outputs back chains passes together, so n written steps allow roughly n x L layers of sequential computation. Coconut keeps this feedback loop but passes a vector instead of a token.

lessons.title: The continuous thought: hidden state in, hidden state out

blocks.md: Coconut's notation: for input tokens $x_1, \dots, x_T$ let $E_t = [e(x_1), \dots, e(x_t)]$ be the input embeddings, $H_t = \text{Transformer}(E_t)$ the last-layer hidden states, and $h_t$ the row for position $t$. A normal model predicts $x_{t+1}$ with $\text{softmax}(W h_t)$, where $W$ is the LM head.

Coconut adds two special tokens. `<bot>` (begin of thought) switches the model into **latent mode** and `<eot>` (end of thought) switches it back to **language mode**. Between them, each input slot receives the previous position's last hidden state. That vector is called a **continuous thought**.

blocks.tex: E_t = [\,e(x_1), \dots, e(x_i),\; h_i,\, h_{i+1}, \dots, h_{t-1}\,] \quad \text{for } i < t < j
blocks.caption: Latent mode with <bot> at position i and <eot> at position j. After j the inputs revert to token embeddings. The paper notes h has already passed the final normalization layer, so its magnitude stays reasonable.

blocks.title: What fills each input slot during latent mode

scenes.caption: A question of 3 tokens, then <bot>, three latent slots, <eot> and the answer. In the official code the slots hold a placeholder <latent> id whose embedding is overwritten before use.
Pass 1 embeds the question and <bot> normally: e(Q1) to e(bot). The last hidden state at position 4, h4, is the first continuous thought.
Pass 2: h4 goes into slot 5 as an input embedding. Its output at position 5, h5, is thought 2. With a KV cache only the new position is computed.
Pass 3: h5 fills slot 6 and produces h6, the third thought. Each thought exists only after the previous pass finishes, so these passes are strictly sequential.
h6 fills slot 7, then <eot> is embedded normally. From here the model is in language mode and decodes the answer token by token, attending to all three thoughts.

blocks.md: During latent mode, $\text{softmax}(W h_t)$ is simply not used: the thought is never mapped back to a word. The paper still computes it as a **probe**, a read-out used only to inspect what a thought encodes, as lesson 4 will show.

blocks.title: Inference with three continuous thoughts

scenes.caption: Simplified from the official Coconut code (which also reuses the KV cache). The question has 3 tokens, so with <bot> the input holds 4 embeddings.
First forward pass. The hidden state at the last position, after the final normalization layer, is thought 1 (h4 in the figure above).
Loop iteration k = 0: append the vector h4 itself, run another pass, read off h5.
Iteration k = 1: append h5, run pass 3, read h6. The loop ran n_thoughts - 1 = 2 times.
Append the last thought and the <eot> embedding: 8 input vectors. Ordinary decoding writes the answer from here.

blocks.md: Training uses the same feedback, which makes it expensive. If a training example has $n$ latent thoughts, Coconut runs $n + 1$ forward passes: one per thought, each producing the next thought, and a final pass that computes the loss on the remaining text. A KV cache avoids recomputing earlier positions, but the passes cannot run in parallel the way teacher-forced token training can.

At inference the model must also know when to leave latent mode. `<bot>` is placed right after the question. For `<eot>` the authors tried a learned binary classifier on the thoughts and simply padding to a fixed number of thoughts; both worked comparably, so the experiments use the fixed length.
Misconception: a continuous thought is not the embedding of the most likely next word. It is never rounded to any vocabulary entry. Decoding it with the LM head is a diagnostic only.
n continuous thoughts cost n sequential forward passes at inference and n + 1 sequential passes per training example, with no tokens emitted for the latent steps.

blocks.question: In latent mode at position t (between <bot> and <eot>), what is the input vector?
options: The embedding of the argmax token of softmax(W h at t-1)
A learned <pause> embedding that is the same at every latent position
The last hidden state h at position t-1, after the final normalization
The average of all previous token embeddings
blocks.explain: Coconut feeds h(t-1) directly. Taking the argmax token would be ordinary greedy CoT, and a fixed learned embedding is what pause tokens do. Only the direct feedback lets each latent input depend on the full previous computation.

blocks.question: The GSM8k Coconut model uses c = 2 thoughts per reasoning step and 3 latent stages, so its final stage has 6 thoughts. How many sequential forward passes does one training example in that stage need?
options: 1, because training uses teacher forcing
blocks.explain: n latent thoughts need n passes to create them plus one more pass to score the remaining tokens: 6 + 1 = 7. Teacher forcing cannot help, because the inputs at the latent slots do not exist until the previous pass has run.

lessons.title: Teaching a model to think without words: the curriculum

blocks.md: The ideal would be to train continuous thoughts end to end from question and answer pairs alone, letting gradient descent discover what a useful thought is. Coconut tried exactly that (the **w/o curriculum** variant) and it did no better than a model that answers immediately. The thoughts need a guide.

The guide comes from earlier work on **implicit chain of thought**. Deng et al. (2023) distilled a CoT teacher so that reasoning happens 'vertically' across a student's layers instead of 'horizontally' across written tokens. Deng, Choi and Shieber (2024) then proposed **Stepwise Internalization (iCoT)**: start from a CoT-trained model and gradually delete CoT tokens from the front of the chain while fine-tuning, until only the answer remains.

blocks.caption: iCoT's linear schedule: s(t) tokens are removed at training step t, with T steps per epoch, so Delta tokens are removed per epoch (Delta = 8 for multiplication: 8, 16, 24 tokens after epochs 1, 2, 3).

blocks.md: iCoT needed two stabilizers. It **resets the optimizer** each time another token is removed, because AdamW's running moment estimates are tuned to the old loss. It also uses **removal smoothing**: remove $s(t) + o$ tokens, with a random offset $P(o) \propto e^{-\lambda o}$. With $\lambda = 4$, $P(o = 0) = 1 - e^{-4} \approx 0.98$, so about 2% of examples preview the next stage. With it, GPT-2 Small reached up to 99% on 9-by-9 multiplication with no written steps.

Coconut adopts the staging idea but swaps the deleted text for thoughts. At stage $k$, the first $k$ reasoning steps are replaced by $k \times c$ continuous thoughts, where $c$ (thoughts per step) is a hyperparameter. If a chain has fewer than $k$ steps, all language steps are removed. Questions and thoughts are masked out of the loss.

blocks.title: The curriculum on one ProsQA example (c = 1)

scenes.caption: Stage 0 is ordinary CoT training. S1 to S3 are 'Tom is a terpus.', 'Every terpus is a brimpus.', 'Every brimpus is a lempus.' The question and markers are masked (-); steps and answer get cross-entropy (CE).
Stage 1: the first language step is removed and replaced by c = 1 continuous thought. The loss is still on S2, S3 and the answer. Nothing asks the thought to reproduce S1.
Stage 2: two steps become two thoughts. The thought positions carry no loss; they are trained only through gradients from the text that follows them.
Stage 3: all three steps are latent, so the model must go from question to answer through thoughts alone. The optimizer state is reset at every stage switch.

ProsQA uses 6 latent stages because the longest chains have 6 steps. Stage k always inserts k thoughts, so in stage 6 this 3-step example has 6 thoughts; pad_latent_to_max keeps 6 in later epochs and at inference instead of trimming to 3.

blocks.md: The objective never asks a thought to compress the step it replaced. Thoughts are trained only by how much they help predict the remaining steps and the answer, so they are free to become something other than a paraphrase of the text.

scenes.caption: GSM8k, GPT-2. Without the curriculum Coconut (14.4) does no better than answering directly (16.5). With it, 34.1. iCoT's 30.0 is quoted from the iCoT paper.
ProsQA. The no-curriculum run again lands at the no-CoT level (76.1 vs 76.7), while every staged method exceeds 95. On this task even staged training without thoughts nearly suffices.

blocks.md: Two controls in the bars isolate the role of thoughts. **Pause as thought** runs the same curriculum but puts fixed `<pause>` tokens in the thought slots; **w/o thought** runs the curriculum with no extra slots at all. On GSM8k both trail real continuous thoughts (24.1 and 21.6 vs 34.1), which the authors read as GSM8k needing the extra computation that chained thoughts provide.

blocks.prompt: On GSM8k, accuracy rose as c went from 0 to 1 to 2 thoughts per step. What do you expect at c = 3?
blocks.reveal: It got slightly **worse**, with higher variance across seeds. The training logs showed a sharp loss spike at stage transitions, especially the last, when three thoughts are added at once. The authors suggest finer schedules that add one thought at a time and remove fewer language tokens, as iCoT does.

blocks.question: A GSM8k Coconut model uses c = 2. In training stage 2, what does an example with 4 reasoning steps look like?
options: Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, steps 3 and 4, answer
Question, <bot>, 4 thoughts, <eot>, answer only
Question, <bot>, 2 thoughts, <eot>, steps 2, 3 and 4, answer
blocks.explain: Stage k removes the first k steps and inserts k x c thoughts: 2 x 2 = 4 thoughts. Steps 3 and 4 remain in language and carry the loss, together with the answer.

blocks.question: Why does Coconut, like iCoT, reset the optimizer state when the training stage changes?
options: To free GPU memory used by the KV cache
Because the loss suddenly changes, and Adam-style moment estimates from the old stage can produce badly scaled updates
Because the vocabulary changes when <bot> and <eot> are added
To force the model to forget the language reasoning steps
blocks.explain: Each stage is effectively a new task: some text targets disappear and new latent slots appear. iCoT found that without resets the accuracy collapsed and did not recover. Coconut follows iCoT and resets at stage switches.

lessons.title: Latent search: one thought, several frontier nodes

blocks.md: To study planning, the Coconut authors built **ProsQA** (Proof with Search Question-Answering). Each question lists 'Every X is a Y' facts that form a directed acyclic graph (DAG) of made-up concepts, then asks 'Is [entity] a [A] or [B]?'. The generator guarantees a path from the entity to A and none to B. On average a graph has 23 nodes and 36 edges, and the shortest solution path has 3.8 steps.

The hard part is the first step. Many edges leave the entity and most lead nowhere useful, so a model that must write its path one step at a time has to guess early, before it can see which branch reaches an answer. Here is a real example from the paper's appendix.

blocks.title: A real ProsQA question as a graph

scenes.caption: The part of the ProsQA appendix example reachable from Tom (other entities like Alex and Davis omitted). Question: 'Is Tom a lempus or scrompus?' scrompus is reachable only from other entities.
Hypothetical greedy CoT: it must write one first step. If it writes 'Tom is a dumpus', it reaches a dead end. In the paper's case study, CoT hit a dead end and then hallucinated an edge.
Latent view, thought 1: one vector can weight both children of Tom at once. Badges show the toy decoder below: 0.50 each. No commitment yet.
Thought 2: the frontier is every node two steps from Tom. dumpus has no children, so its branch simply drops out; nothing had to be undone.
Thought 3: the three-step frontier contains lempus, one of the two options. Now the answer is easy to read off: Tom is a lempus.

blocks.md: Why can a thought keep several branches alive? A vector can be a weighted mix of several concept directions, and decoding it with the LM head spreads probability over all of them. The toy below makes that literal. It is a deliberately simplified model, not Coconut's learned weights.

blocks.title: Toy: decoding a superposed thought with softmax(W h)

scenes.caption: Greedy CoT after step 1: all mass on the single token it wrote, here the unlucky dumpus.
Toy thought 1: h is the normalized sum of the embeddings of terpus and dumpus. With orthonormal embeddings and logits 10 W h, each gets 0.499.
Toy thought 2: four frontier nodes at 0.248 each, 0.002 elsewhere. One vector can hold a set of candidates; a token holds one.
Toy thought 3: the frontier includes lempus. Simplified: real thoughts are not exact sums, and the paper's probes show unequal weights that act like a value estimate.

blocks.md: The paper measured this on the trained model. They force the model out of latent mode after $k$ thoughts and read the probability of each concept it could write next. They treat that probability as an **implicit value function**: the model's estimate that a node leads to the answer.

In the paper's case study (a different graph from the Tom example above, about an entity named Alex), after thought 1 the highest-valued child of Alex was 'lempus' at 0.33. After thought 2 the model gave 0.87 to 'rorpus', a child of a different first-level node, 'grimpus', instead of extending 'lempus'. That is not greedy search. Across the test set, the summed values of the top 1, 2 and 3 candidates differ noticeably after thought 1, a sign of several live options; after thought 2 those gaps narrow.

Why delay the decision? The authors define a node's **height** as its shortest distance to any leaf. Nodes with low height, close to the end of the graph, get sharp and accurate values; high nodes near the start get ambiguous ones. Keeping options open until the frontier is close to the leaves lets the model judge branches where its judgments are reliable.

BFS-like (breadth-first-search-like) is an interpretation from probing, not a built-in algorithm. Coconut was never trained to search, keeps no explicit visited set, and the parallelism narrows after a couple of thoughts.
A continuous thought can encode a weighted set of next steps. Deferring commitment is what let Coconut reach 97.0% on ProsQA where CoT reached 77.5%, while generating 14.2 tokens instead of 49.4.

blocks.question: In the toy, what happens to the dumpus branch between thought 1 and thought 2?
options: The model must emit a backtracking token to undo it
It keeps its 0.50 weight because thoughts cannot forget
It contributes no children to the next frontier, so it fades out without any explicit backtracking
It is moved to the answer slot
blocks.explain: The next frontier is built from the children of the current one. dumpus has none, so its weight goes nowhere. A written CoT that had already said 'Tom is a dumpus' would be stuck with that text in its context.

blocks.question: According to the paper's height analysis, why does postponing the choice help on ProsQA?
options: Later thoughts have more parameters available
Values for nodes close to the leaves are estimated more accurately than for nodes near the start, so later decisions are better informed
The LM head is only accurate after <eot>
Postponing lets the model skip reading the question
blocks.explain: Figure 7 in the paper shows correct and incorrect nodes are well separated at low height but blurred at large height. Exploring forward before committing turns hard early choices into easier late ones.

lessons.title: Pause tokens, filler dots, recurrent depth and Coconut's costs

blocks.md: Coconut is one of several ways to give a model computation that does not appear as readable text. They differ in **what enters the extra input slots** and therefore in what the extra compute can do.

**Pause tokens** (Goyal et al., 2023) append copies of a learned `<pause>` token to the input and ignore the outputs until the last one. Gains appeared mainly when pauses were used in both pretraining and finetuning: for a 1B model, +18% exact match on SQuAD, +8% on CommonSenseQA and +1% on GSM8k over a 7.5% baseline. In Coconut's GPT-2 comparison, the pause baseline matched no-CoT on GSM8k (16.4 vs 16.5).

**Filler tokens**: Pfau, Merrill and Bowman (2024) replaced CoT with meaningless dots ('......'). Small Llama-architecture transformers then solved two synthetic tasks, 3SUM and 2SUM-Transform (100% and 94%), that they failed without filler. But learning to use filler required specific, dense supervision, and theory says a transformer with filler tokens stays in the circuit class $\mathsf{TC}^0$, unlike CoT, which can go beyond it.

scenes.caption: Two positions of one forward pass, simplified. Inside a pass, information moves up one layer at a time and sideways through attention to earlier positions at lower layers.
Pause or filler tokens: position t+1 holds a fixed <pause> or '.' embedding. It adds width (more vectors to attend to), but any path from input to output still climbs at most L layers.
Coconut: the top-layer state at t becomes the input at t+1, so the path runs through all L layers twice. With n thoughts, the serial path is about (n + 1) x L layers, like written CoT.

blocks.md: **Recurrent depth** (Geiping et al., 2025) puts the loop inside the network instead. A **prelude** of layers embeds the input, a **core block** is applied $r$ times starting from a random state with the input re-injected each time, and a **coda** decodes. Training samples $r$ per step from a heavy-tailed distribution and backpropagates through only the last 8 iterations. Unlike Coconut it needs no CoT data. Their 3.5B-parameter model, trained on 800B tokens, kept improving on reasoning benchmarks as test-time recurrences grew.

scenes.caption: With GPT-2's 12 layers, Coconut's 6 ProsQA thoughts put 7 x 12 = 84 layers on the serial path. Pause tokens stay at 12 however many you add.
Geiping et al.'s recurrent model has 2 prelude, 4 recurrent and 2 coda layers. At its training mean of 32 recurrences that is 2 + 32 x 4 + 2 = 132 effective layers, the figure the paper reports.
Simplified: serial depth is an upper bound on sequential computation, not a quality score. Slide L to see a deeper base model.
GSM8k: written CoT still wins (42.9) over Coconut (34.1), but CoT generates 25.0 tokens vs Coconut's 8.2, about 3.05 times more. iCoT's 30.0 is from the iCoT paper.
ProntoQA: Coconut 99.8 vs CoT 98.8 with 9.0 tokens instead of 92.5. Measured on an A100 at batch size 1: 0.11 s vs 0.85 s per case, about 7.7 times faster.
ProsQA, the search-heavy task: Coconut 97.0 vs CoT 77.5. Plain CoT barely beats no-CoT (76.7) here, while staged latent methods all exceed 95.

blocks.md: The costs are real. Training needs $n + 1$ sequential passes per example, which the authors flag as a parallelism problem. The curriculum depends on written CoT data to start from. On GSM8k, CoT still beats Coconut on accuracy. On larger models the gain over no-CoT shrank: Llama 3.2-3B went from 26.0 to 31.7 and Llama 3-8B from 42.2 to 43.6, possibly because heavy language pretraining makes the switch to latent inputs harder.

Loss of auditability is a design cost, not a detail. Latent thoughts can be probed with the LM head, but there is no readable trace to check. Pfau et al. raise the same concern: hidden computation can drift away from anything a human, or a behavior-based safety check, can read.

Choose by what the extra slots carry. Fixed pause or filler embeddings add width within one pass. Coconut's fed-back hidden states and written CoT add serial depth across passes. Recurrent depth adds serial depth inside the network without any extra tokens.

blocks.question: Your team must ship a math tutor whose reasoning is reviewed by teachers for errors. Which approach fits best?
options: Coconut with 6 continuous thoughts, since it is faster
Pause tokens, since they need no CoT data
Written chain-of-thought, accepting the extra tokens, because reviewers need a readable trace
Recurrent depth with r = 64, since it has more effective layers
blocks.explain: Every latent method trades away a readable trace. When humans must audit the reasoning, written CoT is the only option here that provides one. It also had the highest GSM8k accuracy in Coconut's own table (42.9 vs 34.1).

blocks.question: Adding 6 pause tokens vs. adding 6 Coconut thoughts to a 12-layer model: what happens to the longest serial chain of layer computations before the answer?
options: Both grow to 84 layers
Pause: stays 12. Coconut: grows to about 84
Pause: grows to 84. Coconut: stays 12
Both stay at 12 because attention is parallel
blocks.explain: A pause slot's input is a fixed embedding, so its computation happens in the same pass and every path climbs at most 12 layers. Each Coconut thought is the top-layer output of the previous pass fed in at the bottom, so 6 thoughts plus the final pass give 7 x 12 = 84.
